newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania farming, investment seen as keys to growth.
newsitem.headline: Romania farming, investment seen as keys to growth.

text.p: Romania should be able to meet projected growth in its economy next year if agriculture recovers and it enjoys increased investment, analysts said.
The National Forecasting Board (CNP) projected gross domestic product would grow 5.5 percent in 1997, from 4.8 percent forecast for this year.

"It is realistic on the assumption that agriculture will put on a better performance in 1997 than this year, which looks like the worst year in a long time," Charlie Robertson from London-based Hilfe economic and political analysis company, told Reuters by phone.
An early winter and spring snowfalls caused heavy losses to farming this year. Wheat output was half last year's 7.8 million tonnes and lower output for other crops is also expected.
Robertson said "more massive investment" would also be needed to push GDP higher.
The board projected 12-month inflation would decline to 20 percent from 30 percent expected this year.
Romanian economist Ilie Serbanescu said, however: "The 1997 GDP growth is attainable but might be costly, at the expense of higher inflation."
He said Romania could be content with lower growth of, say, two percent, as long as this was export-led.
Romanian exports have been on the slide this year, with an eight-month figure down some 10 percent from the same 1995 period.
Serbanescu doubted a 20 percent inflation target could be achieved. "We will have 20 percent inflation next year the way we had 20 percent inflation this year."

Romania expects inflation of about 30 percent this year, a level revised recently from a previous estimate of 20 percent, but local economists say the 12-month figure will be higher than the revised forecast due to hefty rises in energy and fuel prices in July.

In July, electricity and thermal power prices rose by 58 percent and fuel prices by approximately 30 percent sending year-on-year inflation up to 40.3 percent from 33.8 percent in June. August's 12-month inflation was 44.2 percent.
"The burden of July's price hikes will be at its worst in the roughest winter months of January and February, which means next year," a local analyst said.
"The effects of prices and a leu exchange rate kept under control for election purposes will be felt in 1997 and targeted inflation will be exceeded," he said.
Romania held local elections in June and will have parliamentary and presidential polls on November 3.

After months of lingering below 3,000 to the dollar this year, the leu breached that sensitive threshold only recently, though currency shops have traded it at around 3,500 for months, which analysts say is more realistic.
Last year Romania cut inflation to 27.8 percent from 61.7 in 1994 and almost 300 percent in 1993. It saw a 6.9 percent GDP growth, up from 3.9 percent in 1994. -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
